title: Households throw away about a sixth of the subsidised bread they buy; the World Bank and FAO name the universal cereal price subsidy as a driver, though household surveys find little direct price effect

rootCauses.cause: Universal consumer price subsidy on bread, flour and other cereal products (compensation since 1945, CGC since 1970), with the retail bread price last raised in 2008 and consumer prices cut symbolically in January 2011 and unchanged since, keeps bread far below cost and removes the price signal against over-buying
Subsidy paid on volume encourages processors and bakeries to produce more than is eaten; bakeries receive flour at a negative price
Household practices: misjudging quantities, over-buying, cooking more than needed, unplanned purchases
Variable flour and bread quality (bread stales quickly), cited as a possible cause by the FAO/ministry chain study and by survey respondents

author: TahaGHZ
excerpt: Tunisian households throw away a large share of the bread they buy. The Institut National de la Consommation (INC) estimated in 2014 that about 900,000 loaves were thrown away each day, equal to 102,000 tonnes and 100…

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content: Tunisian households throw away a large share of the bread they buy. The Institut National de la Consommation (INC) estimated in 2014 that about 900,000 loaves were thrown away each day, equal to 102,000 tonnes and 100 million TND a year (SRC-TG-906). Its May-June 2016 household surveys put bread waste at 42 kg per household a year, 113,000 tonnes in total, or 15.7% of the bread households buy (SRC-TG-906, SRC-TG-907). An INC study published in 2019, cited by the World Bank, gives 16% of bread bought and 10% of cereals; its survey year is not stated (SRC-TG-903). A 2025 peer-reviewed paper cites INC (2025) for the same 113,000 t, about 16% of household bread expenditure and 5% of food expenditure (SRC-TG-911), and 2026 press repeats them (SRC-TG-910); since the values are unchanged, the current level is not newly measured. By waste rate, bread is the most wasted food in every INC figure we found. Waste rises in Ramadan: 46% of INC respondents name bread among the foods most wasted then, after cooked dishes (66.6%); these are shares of respondents, not waste rates (SRC-TG-906). Total household food waste was valued at 570-572 million TND a year in 2018 (SRC-TG-909, SRC-TG-907). Since over 80% of soft wheat is imported (SRC-TG-901, SRC-TG-907; other sources give a higher share, see FND-TG-700), much of the wasted bread was bought abroad with foreign currency.

sections.heading: Root causes
sections.content:
**Symptom vs cause.** The 900,000 loaves is the symptom. The evidence names three layers of cause.

1. **Past policy: universal cereal price subsidy (legacy decision).** Consumer price compensation dates from 1945 and the Caisse Générale de Compensation was set up in 1970 (SRC-TG-903; the institutional history is in FND-TG-702). The World Bank's 2022 monitor says the retail bread price has not been raised since 2008, and that consumer prices of subsidised goods were cut symbolically on the eve of 14 January 2011 and not adjusted since (SRC-TG-903). The two statements are compatible. The World Bank concludes that low prices gave Tunisia a world record for wheat consumption per head, more than double the world average, that some bread is fed to livestock because it is cheaper than feed, and that the subsidy structure produces "overconsumption at the household level" and "significant leakages and waste" (SRC-TG-903). The World Bank's 2024 project paper names wastage of 900,000 baguettes daily among the system's distortions (SRC-TG-705). The FAO/ministry chain study says products sold well below cost "incite au gaspillage" and lists "les prix dérisoires au niveau consommateur" among possible causes of bread waste (SRC-TG-901).
2. **Supply-side incentives.** Subsidies are paid on volumes, so processors have an incentive to produce more to receive more subsidy (SRC-TG-903). Bakeries buy flour from mills at a negative price and are also subsidised for water, electricity and labour (SRC-TG-903).
3. **Household behaviour and bread quality.** INC respondents name over-buying (87.9%), cooking too much (87.3%) and unplanned purchases (84%) as the main causes (SRC-TG-906). In a 2023 online survey of 320 Tunisians, 61.5% named misjudging the quantity bought, 12.8% bread quality, 9% poor storage and 2.6% over-production (SRC-TG-911). The FAO/ministry study suggests flour quality and bakery processes may also explain bread waste (SRC-TG-901); in 2016, 56% of INC respondents rated subsidised bread quality as average or poor (SRC-TG-906).

**Evidence that complicates the subsidy explanation.** In the same INC survey, 73% of respondents said the current bread price does not encourage them to buy more than they need, and only 1-2% knew the real size of the subsidy on the baguette or "gros pain" (SRC-TG-906). An independent peer-reviewed survey (Sept-Dec 2023, convenience sample of 320 Tunisians, mostly university-educated women) found only 14.1% of respondents named government subsidies as a main cause, described bread wastage as "limited" (5.8% consistently discard stored bread), and "found no direct correlation between perceived price and waste" (SRC-TG-911). The price link therefore rests on the World Bank's cross-country reasoning and the FAO/ministry SWOT statement, not on household evidence. Low price may work by making waste feel costless rather than by conscious over-buying, but no Tunisian study tests this.

sections.heading: Evidence
sections.content:
- Bread waste volume, two INC estimates: 102,000 t/year (2014 estimate from 900,000 loaves a day) and 113,000 t/year (2016 surveys, 42 kg per household, 2.7 million households) (SRC-TG-906, SRC-TG-907).
- Share of bread wasted: 15.7% of bread purchased (2016 surveys, SRC-TG-906; SRC-TG-907); 16% of bread bought (INC study published 2019, SRC-TG-903; also in 2026 press, SRC-TG-910); about 16% of household bread expenditure (INC 2025 as cited in SRC-TG-911).
- Value: 100 million TND a year for bread (SRC-TG-906). Total household food waste: "over 570 million TND" (Minister of Trade, December 2018, SRC-TG-909), 572 million TND (INC via TAP, November 2018, SRC-TG-907), 570 million TND (2026 press, SRC-TG-910).
- **Share of food spending wasted, sources disagree:** 5% of household food spending, or 17 TND per household per month (INC 2016 surveys, SRC-TG-906; repeated in SRC-TG-907, SRC-TG-910) vs 18% of food spending (INC study published in 2019, as cited in a World Bank footnote, SRC-TG-903). We could not see either INC report to reconcile them.
- **UNEP Food Waste Index:** household food waste of 88 kg per capita in 2019 (very low confidence) and 172 kg per capita, 2.12 million tonnes, in 2022 (medium confidence) (SRC-TG-900). The jump is a change of method and confidence class between the 2021 and 2024 editions, not a trend. The UNEP figures include inedible parts and cover all foods, so they are not comparable with INC bread figures. They do suggest household waste in Tunisia is not small.
- **Cost of the subsidy that is wasted:** food subsidy spending rose from 730 million TND in 2010 to 2,569 million TND in 2020, and cereals took over three quarters of direct food subsidies in 2020 (SRC-TG-903). The cereal subsidy line in the FAO/ministry study was 887 million TND in 2011 and 1,286 million TND in 2016 (SRC-TG-901). The bread or bread-flour subsidy was reported at 400 million TND and 450 million TND for 2017 in two INC statements (SRC-TG-906, SRC-TG-907). If 15.7% of bread is wasted, a comparable share of the bread subsidy is spent on bread that is thrown away; this is our inference, not a sourced figure.

sections.heading: Why confidence is what it is
sections.content: Medium. The existence and rough size of bread waste are supported beyond the press: the 900,000 loaves a day, 100 million TND and 16% figures appear in tier B reports (World Bank, FAO/ministry), and 113,000 t, about 16% and 5% of food spending appear in a tier A peer-reviewed paper (SRC-TG-911), though only as a restatement of INC figures (one co-author works at the INC), not as an independent measurement. Claims still resting only on tier C press reports: 102,000 t a year, 42 kg per household, 15.7% of bread purchased, 570-572 million TND, and the 400 and 450 million TND bread subsidy figures. The causal attribution to the subsidy is contested: the World Bank and FAO/ministry name it, while two household surveys (SRC-TG-906, SRC-TG-911) find little direct price effect. All INC figures reach us second-hand (press, or World Bank and FAO reports citing them), come from surveys of 2014-2016 (2019 at the latest) with unknown samples, and disagree on the share of food spending (5% vs 18%) and on volume (102,000 vs 113,000 t). The UNEP estimate is modelled and its 2022 value rests on a study we could not identify. The subsidy-causes-waste link is contradicted by household self-reports (SRC-TG-906, SRC-TG-911).

sections.heading: Links to other sectors
sections.content:
- Energy: bakeries' electricity is subsidised as part of the cereal subsidy chain (SRC-TG-903), so subsidised energy goes into bread that is thrown away. No source quantifies this.
- Water: bakeries' water is also subsidised as part of the same chain (SRC-TG-903), so subsidised water goes into bread that is thrown away. Not quantified; no Tunisian source quantifies the water embedded in wasted bread.
- Waste management: the INC says 68% of household waste is organic and only 5% of it is recycled (SRC-TG-907); wasted bread adds to this stream.

sections.heading: Leads for phase 2
sections.content:
- INC national strategy against food waste with FAO and the Ministry of Trade, started February 2025, diagnostic report validated 13 May 2026, workshops 10 and 17 June 2026 (SRC-TG-910)
- FAO/AICS project GCP/RNE/004/ITA second phase (2018): training of bakers, university canteen managers and teachers, awareness for pupils and rural women (SRC-TG-909)
- INC proposal for a national anti-waste day (SRC-TG-909)
- World Bank proposal to replace universal cereal price subsidies with cash transfers to households (SRC-TG-903); grain value chain reform measures under the Tunisia Emergency Food Security Response Project (SRC-TG-705; detail in FND-TG-702)
- FAO "guide des bonnes pratiques contre le gaspillage alimentaire" for Tunisia (seen in search results, not opened)
- Food bank or bread redistribution schemes: none found in this search

resolvedSources.extracts:
Dated March 1, 2024. Sectoral context, para 8, p. 3:

> For the fourth consecutive year, below-average rainfall and extreme heat have combined to dramatically compromise Tunisia's grain production in 2022/23. As shown in Table 1 below, the Grain Board collected less than half of durum wheat quantities in 2023 compared to average drought years 2020-22 and two-thirds less than in a non-drought year (such as 2019), and almost no barley (1.3 percent of average drought years).

Table 1, "Grain quantities collected by OC (2019-2023)", '000 t, source Tunisia Grain Board (OC), rows (2019 / average 2020-2022 / 2023):

> Durum wheat 876.4 685.6 286.7
> Soft wheat 75.4 31.3 6.2
> Barley 332.9 39.5 0.5
> Total 1284.7 756.4 293.4

Para 8, p. 3 (continued):

> Consequently, average monthly grain import needs have skyrocketed (100,000 MT/month for durum wheat and 100,000 MT/month for barley, currently estimated at US$48 million/month for durum wheat and US$28 million/month for barley).

Footnote 15:

> This is particularly true in Tunisia where people remember vividly the bread riots that occurred from December 1983 to January 1984, triggered by a temporary rise in the price of bread due to the government austerity program.

Para 9, p. 3:

> For the period from July 2023 to June 2024, the Grain Board is facing an additional financing gap of around US$522 million due to very low local harvest of durum wheat and barley.

Footnote to Table 2, p. 4:

> Soft wheat import needs are not substantially impacted by drought since Tunisia is 95 percent dependent on imports.

Box 1, p. 4:

> The Grain Board (OC) is an SOE created in 1962 under the tutelage of Ministry of Agriculture, Water Resources and Fisheries (MAWRF) with a core mandate to regulate and ensure a stable supply of grain on the domestic market through domestic grain harvest collection, imports, and the management of strategic reserves.

> The OC has a de jure monopoly over grain trade (domestic collection and imports), except for barley (animal feed) for which domestic collection (traditionally) and imports (since April 2023) have been authorized for selected private operators.

> The OC buys grain domestically at farmgate prices fixed annually by a government decree. These prices have been below import-parity prices; they were increased by around 60 percent since 2022 to incentivize production.

> The OC sells the grain it purchases at subsidized prices to the millers who are granted specific acquisition quotas; the millers in turn sell the milled products (soft wheat bread flour, soft wheat pastry flour, durum semolina) to bakeries and processors similarly at subsidized prices under quota assignments. End products (such as bread, pasta, and couscous) are sold to consumers at subsidized prices.

> Because of CGC protracted payments, OC must resort to financing by the National Agriculture Bank which is difficult to mobilize and costly.

> CGC, a state-owned entity created in 1970, is responsible for providing compensatory payments to operators at the different segments of the grain value chain to cover the gap between market and administered prices.

Footnote 3:

> Farmgate gate prices in 2023 have been increased by 60.9 percent, 64.2 percent and 60.7 percent for durum wheat, soft wheat and barley respectively, compared to 2021. In February 2024, official farmgate prices for durum wheat and barley are respectively 3 percent sand 14 percent lower than OC import cost (Source OC).

Box 1 continued, p. 5:

> (iii) there are illegal and improper use of subsidized grain products, i.e., improper use of semolina for feed to animals, illegal leakages of grain products towards neighboring countries, as well as excessive consumption and wastage of bread and wheat-based products by end-consumers, e.g., wastage of 900,000 "baguettes" daily; and (iv) the system limits the active participation of the private sector

Para 10, p. 5:

> For calendar years 2022 and 2023, the OC was supposed to receive TND6,625 million (Tunisian Dinar) – i.e., approximately US$2,106 million - from the CGC, but funding effectively received from the compensation fund was only 38 percent (i.e., TND2,543 million or US$808 million).

> As of February 2024, the OC's estimated overall 2023 balance (yet to be audited) amounts to TND -900 million (equivalent to US$ -286 million) and OC's total debt to commercial banks is TND6,343 million (equivalent to US$2,016 million, out of which 83 percent towards the National Agriculture Bank - BNA).

Para 11, p. 5:

> the GoT is carrying out a series of measures that, if fully implemented, would lead to a more sustainable sector and sizeable budget savings in the range of US$400-600 million per year.

Para 10, p. 5 (continued):

> This situation makes it very difficult for OC to access additional financing from commercial banks for grain imports

Para 13:

> This series of reforms would lead to OC's budget and fiscal savings estimated at US$576 million per year

Table 3, "Summary reform measures of the grain value chain and associated savings", measure names (rows extracted as text; fiscal columns not used):

> 4 Strengthening of compensation for losses (FIDAC) [...] Approved (2024 Fiscal Law)- December 31, 2023
> 5 Improved access to seasonal credit for grain producers [...] Approved (2024 Fiscal Law)- December 31, 2023
> 9 Liberalization of soft wheat imports for industrial processing of pastry flour (PS-7) [...] Planned: Cabinet Council to review the draft Decision

Footnote 4 (to Table 3 measure "Strengthening of compensation for losses (FIDAC)", approved in the 2024 Fiscal Law):

> FIDAC (Fonds d'Indemnisation des Dommages Agricoles causés par les Calamités naturelles): is a farmers' compensation fund in case of natural disaster, including drought.

Results framework, p. 43:

> Food subsidy reform implementation plan prepared [...] Preparation of a reform plan for food subsidies and switch to cash transfer, including consultation and communication.

Footnote 17:

> 43.3 percent of bread subsidy for "Gros pain" and 43.5 percent of subsidy for other staple durum wheat-based products go to the poorest two quintiles of Tunisia households in 2022.
resolvedSources.notes: Donor project document; figures on OC finances are sourced to the OC itself and are unaudited. Table 1 rows extracted cleanly; Table 2 (financing gap) extracted with shifted columns and is not used except for its footnote. Table 3 lists nine reform measures (barley import liberalisation April 2023, farmgate price increases, PS-7 flour taxation, planned soft wheat import liberalisation for pastry flour) — recorded as phase 2 leads only.

resolvedSources.notes:
- Food waste here includes inedible parts (bones, peels), per the UNEP definition. It is not comparable with "edible bread thrown away" figures.
- The 2019 and 2022 values come from two editions with different methods and confidence classes. The jump from 88 to 172 kg is not a trend. The change from "Very Low" to "Medium" confidence suggests the 2024 edition used at least one measured data point for Tunisia or a nearby country, but the UNEP report PDF itself (wedocs.unep.org) was behind a Cloudflare challenge and could not be opened to check which study.
- No Food Loss Index (12.3.1a) value exists for Tunisia in the database.

resolvedSources.title: Analyse de la filière céréalière en Tunisie et identification des principaux points de dysfonctionnement à l'origine des pertes (Version finale), projet GCP/RNE/004/ITA
resolvedSources.publisher: FAO / Ministère de l'Agriculture (MARHP), authors R. Khaldi and B. Saaidia; hosted by ONAGRI
resolvedSources.extracts:
PDF p. 7 (Contexte de l'étude):

> Dans la région du Proche-Orient et de l'Afrique du Nord, les pertes et gaspillages au niveau de la filière céréalière sont estimés par la FAO à 19 %. Une étude récente, réalisée par l'INC en Tunisie, portant sur le gaspillage du pain, a montré que 900.000 unités de pain sont gaspillées par jour, soit une valeur 100 millions de dinars ($50 million) par an.

> l'importation de plus de 80% des besoins en blé tendre, soit 4 baguettes sur 5 sont importées !

English gloss: FAO estimates cereal-chain losses and waste in the Near East and North Africa at 19% (regional, not Tunisian). A recent INC study found 900,000 bread units wasted per day, worth 100 million dinars a year. Over 80% of soft wheat needs are imported.

PDF p. 12 and p. 34 (Résumé; Collecte):

> La collecte représente, selon les années, entre 40 et 50% de la récolte

English gloss: Collection represents 40-50% of the harvest depending on the year.

PDF p. 56 (Régulation à travers la CGC):

> Il reçoit à cette fin des fonds de la CGC qui permettent de subventionner des opérations de « vente à perte » en raison du décalage entre les prix perçus et les coûts réels. Ainsi, la plus grande partie des frais de logistique et de stockage des céréales est à la charge de l'État.

PDF p. 57:

> En 2007, les charges de compensation ont connu une forte hausse pour les céréales s'élevant à 472 millions de dinars contre 239,5 millions de dinars en 2006

> Les subventions des prix des céréales ont plafonné depuis 2007, atteignant en 2015 une part de 85% du total des charges de compensation des produits alimentaires (tableau 11).

Tableau 11 rows (subsidised quantities): "Blé tendre (million Qx) 10.96 11.2 11.3 11.4 11.726 11.596" for 2011-2016.

Tableau 11 (cereal subsidy amount, million dinars): 2011 887.397; 2012 1010.499; 2013 1134.295; 2014 1166.411; 2015 1392.159; 2016 1286.323.

English gloss: The Office des Céréales receives CGC funds to cover "sales at a loss"; most grain logistics and storage costs are borne by the state. Cereal compensation rose to 472 MD in 2007 from 239.5 MD in 2006 and reached 85% of food compensation in 2015.

PDF p. 61-62 (SWOT, transformation):

> Des produits sont offerts bien en dessous de leur prix de revient, ce qui incite au gaspillage.

> Il existe énormément de gaspillage au niveau de la consommation du pain, qui pourrait avoir plusieurs causes comme la qualité de la matière première (farine), les procédés de fabrication du pain au niveau

English gloss: Products are sold well below cost, which encourages waste. There is a great deal of bread waste at consumption, which could have several causes such as flour quality and bakery processes.

PDF p. 70 (Pertes à la récolte):

> En Tunisie, la récolte mécanique des céréales est malheureusement réputée pour les importantes pertes qu'elle occasionne. Pour donner un exemple, si les pertes sont de l'ordre de 10%, sur une année moyenne (17 millions de quintaux), le volume total des pertes serait de 1,7millions de quintaux.

> En Tunisie, 60% des machines agricoles sont âgées de plus de 25 ans, ce qui occasionne une perte de 100 millions de dinars par an (MARH, 2017).

English gloss: Mechanical harvesting is known for large losses; the 10% figure is a hypothetical example, not a measurement. 60% of farm machines are over 25 years old, causing a loss of 100 MD a year (citing the ministry, 2017).

PDF p. 71-72 (Stockage à la ferme; Collecte):

> Cette différence comprend vraisemblablement des pertes qu'il est très difficile de quantifier chez les agriculteurs.

> La fréquence du stockage en plein air ou dans des silos australiens sans respect des conditions minimales de stockage dont notamment une couverture adéquat du stock,

> L'utilisation quasi-totale des sacs plastiques abimables facilement lors des manutentions

> Lorsque la capacité de stockage est insuffisante ou en année pluvieuse accompagnée d'une bonne récolte, une augmentation du stockage ponctuel à l'air libre est souvent préconisée. Cette pratique peut être à l'origine de pertes importantes : prédateurs, consommation par les oiseaux, retrait de produits impropres lors d'épisodes pluvieux, ou même vols.

English gloss: The gap between harvest and collection probably contains losses that are very hard to quantify on farms. Collection centres often store grain in the open or in uncovered bunker ("Australian") silos, use fragile plastic sacks, and resort to open-air storage in big harvest years, causing losses to pests, birds, rain and theft.

PDF p. 61 (SWOT, première transformation):

> L'OC ne rémunère pas le stockage lorsqu'il est assuré par les minotiers : Ces derniers n'investissent pas suffisamment dans les silos de stockage.

English gloss: The Office des Céréales does not pay millers for storage, so they under-invest in silos.

PDF p. 72 (Stockage à la ferme; Collecte):

> Ce mode de stockage est adopté par les agriculteurs qui souhaitent vendre progressivement leurs céréales sur le marché ou attendre un acheteur. Toutefois, ces derniers ne sont pas encadrés, ni formés sur les bonnes pratiques du stockage.

> L'entrée des privés à la sphère de la collecte reste ponctuelle et ressemble surtout à une sous-traitance plutôt qu'une véritable privatisation de l'activité.

English gloss: Farmers who store grain to sell gradually are neither supported nor trained in good storage practice. Private entry into collection looks like sub-contracting rather than real privatisation.

PDF p. 94 (Conclusion, Bizerte and Siliana):

> on relève l'absence de coordination entre les agriculteurs et les centres de collecte liée à plusieurs facteurs pouvant être à l'origine des pertes : - Pratique de contractualisation peu développée - Faible pouvoir de négociation des agriculteurs, notamment en ce qui concerne les services rendus par les propriétaires de matériel de récolte - Dominance de la petite agriculture à faible accès aux services d'appui technique et financier et peu organisée - Présence d'un circuit parallèle formé par des intermédiaires et d'un circuit informel

English gloss: In Bizerte and Siliana, there is no coordination between farmers and collection centres: little contracting, weak bargaining power of farmers over harvest-machinery owners, predominance of small poorly supported farms, and a parallel circuit of intermediaries and informal trade.

PDF p. 94 (Conclusion):

> A ce jour, peu de données existent en Tunisie sur l'ampleur des pertes aux différents stades de la filière céréalière et peu de pratiques et organisations sont mises en oeuvre pour limiter ces pertes

English gloss: To date, few data exist in Tunisia on the scale of losses at the different stages of the cereal chain.
resolvedSources.notes:
- Phase 1 (diagnostic) report of the FAO/Italy project. It states that loss quantification is the subject of a second phase; that phase 2 report (Bizerte and Siliana estimates) was not found online.
- No date printed on the cover; the latest data cited are from August 2017 and the 2017 investment code decrees, so it is dated 2017 here (possibly finalised in 2018).
- The 18% and 27% cumulative loss figures on PDF p. 67-68 describe France (ADEME / INCOME Consulting 2016), not Tunisia, and are not used.

resolvedSources.title: Bulletin de conjoncture de l'économie tunisienne / Tunisia Economic Monitor, Summer 2022: Gérer la crise en temps d'incertitude (Part B: Les subventions des céréales)
resolvedSources.extracts:
Part B, p. 17 (PDF p. 35):

> Ces biens comprennent principalement le pain, la farine, la semoule, les pâtes alimentaires, le lait, l'huile végétale. Le prix de détail du pain, par exemple, n'a pas été augmenté depuis 2008 (voir l'exemple) malgré une augmentation considérable des coûts des intrants de production (notamment le blé, la main-d'oeuvre, les loyers, l'énergie etc.).

English gloss: Subsidised goods are mainly bread, flour, semolina, pasta, milk and vegetable oil. The retail price of bread has not been raised since 2008 despite large increases in input costs.

p. 18 (PDF p. 36):

> Le système de compensation remonte à 1945 et la caisse générale de compensation, structure administrative chargée de gérer le système a été créé en 1970.

> En 2020, les céréales accaparaient plus des trois quarts des subventions totales directes des produits alimentaires.

> Par ailleurs, les gouvernements successifs n'ont pas ajusté les prix aux consommateurs depuis 2011. Les prix ont même été symboliquement réduits la veille du 14 Janvier 2011 sans aucun changement depuis.

> En effet, les prix faibles de détail des céréales et dérivés ont contribué à enregistrer un record mondial pour la Tunisie en termes de consommation de blé par habitant. Celle-ci dépassant le double de la moyenne mondiale. Une partie du pain produite sert même d'alimentation pour bétails car le pain est moins cher que les produits qui leurs sont destinés.

> Cette demande extrêmement élevée de céréales reflète également les incitations des transformateurs à produire plus (pour recevoir plus de subventions) et génère un fort gaspillage des produits céréaliers.

> En effet, entre 2010 et 2020, la subvention des produits alimentaires est passée de 730 MD à 2569 MD

Footnote 11, p. 18:

> Une étude de l'Institut National de la Consommation publie en 2019 estime que le gaspillage alimentaire coûte à chaque tunisien en moyenne 18% du total des dépenses alimentaires. Le pain figure en première position parmi les produits gaspillés par les Tunisiens, avec un taux de 16% des pains achetés, suivi par les céréales (10%).

English gloss: The compensation system dates from 1945; the CGC was created in 1970. Cereals took over three quarters of direct food subsidies in 2020. Consumer prices have not been adjusted since 2011 (they were even cut symbolically on the eve of 14 January 2011). Low prices helped give Tunisia a world record in wheat consumption per head, over double the world average; some bread is fed to livestock because it is cheaper than feed. Processor incentives to produce more (to receive more subsidy) generate heavy waste of cereal products. Food subsidies rose from 730 MD (2010) to 2,569 MD (2020). An INC study published in 2019 is cited as finding food waste costs 18% of food spending, with bread first at 16% of bread bought, then cereals at 10%.

Executive summary (English), p. xiii-xiv:

> The structure of subsidies has also encouraged overproduction--at the processor level--and overconsumption--at the household level--of cereals, generating significant leakages and waste.

Encadré, p. 20 (PDF p. 38):

> Dans le cas des boulangeries, la subvention est tellement importante qu'elles achètent la farine aux minoteries à un prix négatif, c'est-à-dire que non seulement les minoteries paient les boulangeries pour acheter la farine mais aussi que les boulangeries sont subventionnées pour payer leurs inputs (eau, électricité mais aussi la main d'oeuvre).

English gloss: Bakeries buy flour from mills at a negative price, and are also subsidised for their inputs (water, electricity, labour).
resolvedSources.notes:
- The same report gives two dates for the consumer price freeze: "depuis 2008" (bread retail price, p. 17) and "depuis 2011" (consumer prices of subsidised goods, p. 18). Both are recorded.
- The 18% share of food spending attributed to an INC 2019 study conflicts with the 5% INC figure reported in the press (SRC-TG-906, SRC-TG-907); the INC report itself was not available.
- The waste and livestock-feed statements are qualitative; the report gives no tonnage for them.

resolvedSources.title: INC : 113 mille tonnes par an de pain gaspillées par les ménages
resolvedSources.extracts:
Article of 25 May 2017 reporting an INC presentation:

> Présentés aujourd'hui par Tarek Ben Jazia, Directeur général de l'INC, les principaux résultats de ces enquêtes et sondages, réalisés durant les mois de mai et juin 2016, ont démontré que 71,3% des personnes sondées affirment que le niveau de gaspillage en Tunisie est élevé.

> Ainsi, le pain et les produits céréaliers accaparent la part du lion du gaspillage chez les ménages, avec respectivement 15,7% et 10,2% contre 2,3% des produits laitiers.

> En valeur, la moyenne du gaspillage alimentaire par ménage par mois est estimée à 17 dinars, soit 5% des dépenses alimentaires.

> L'INC a dévoilé que les principales sources de gaspillage alimentaire se résument principalement dans l'achat excessif avec 87,9%%, la préparation excessive par rapport aux besoins avec 87,3% et les achats non planifiés avec 84%.

> Au volet de la consommation du pain en Tunisie, l'INC a dévoilé qu'en 2014, les estimations tablent autour de 900 000 pains jetés quotidiennement pour un coût évalué à 300 000 dinars, soit l'équivalent de 102 mille tonnes et de 100 millions de dinars par an.

> Les résultats des enquêtes récentes ont démontré que le reste du pain non consommé par ménage par an représente 42 kg pour un total de 113 mille tonnes par an.

> Le gaspillage du pain est de plus en plus élevé en Tunisie, et ce, malgré le fait que 73% des personnes enquêtées précisent que le niveau actuel des prix du pain n'encourage pas à en acheter plus que de besoin.

> Dans le même sillage, 44% des interrogés ont indiqué que la qualité du pain subventionné est bonne, contre 43% de qualité moyenne et 13% de mauvaise qualité. Sachant que 2% uniquement des Tunisiens connaissent la vraie valeur de la subvention allouée au Grand pain et 1% pour la Baguette. Sachant également que 400 millions de dinars correspondent au montant alloué pour subventionner à l'année la farine de pain.

> Pendant le mois de Ramadan, le gaspillage alimentaire augmente. D'ailleurs, 66,6% des personnes sondées ont dévoilé que les plats cuisinés se taillent la part du lion du gaspillage. Suivent le pain avec 46%, les fruits avec 31,7%

Reference box: "Sur un total de 2,7 millions de ménages à fin 2015 ... Pain : 73kg; Baguettes : 105 pièces; Gros pains : 112 pièces."

English gloss: INC surveys of May-June 2016. Households waste 15.7% of bread and 10.2% of cereal products (2.3% of dairy). Average waste is 17 dinars per household per month, 5% of food spending. Main self-reported causes: over-buying (87.9%), over-cooking (87.3%), unplanned purchases (84%). An INC 2014 estimate put bread thrown away at 900,000 loaves a day (300,000 dinars a day), equal to 102 thousand tonnes and 100 MD a year; recent surveys give 42 kg per household per year, 113 thousand tonnes in total. 73% of respondents say the current bread price does not encourage buying more than needed. 44% rate subsidised bread quality good, 43% average, 13% poor; 2% know the real subsidy on "gros pain", 1% on the baguette; 400 MD a year subsidises bread flour. In Ramadan, 66.6% of respondents name cooked dishes as the most wasted item, 46% name bread (shares of respondents, not waste rates).
resolvedSources.notes:
- Press report of an INC presentation; the INC survey report itself was not available (inc.nat.tn had an expired TLS certificate). Sample size not given.
- The 900,000 loaves per day figure is an INC estimate for 2014. It is repeated unchanged by the FAO/ministry study around 2017 (SRC-TG-901) and in 2026 press (SRC-TG-910), so later dates are restatements, not new measurements.

resolvedSources.title: هذه قيمة التبذير الغذائي في تونس (TAP dispatch on INC food waste figures)
resolvedSources.extracts:
Article dated 20 November 2018 (datePublished 2018-11-20):

> يبلغ حجم التبذير الغذائي على مستوى الأسر التونسية 5 بالمائة من إجمالي النفقات الغذائية، في السنة، أي ما يعادل 572 مليون دينار، وفق المعهد الوطني للاستهلاك.

English gloss: Household food waste equals 5% of total food spending a year, i.e. about 572 million dinars, according to the INC.

> وتظهر دراسات وبحوث المعهد، أنّ حجم تبذير الخبز لدى الأسر التونسية (2.7 مليون أسرة) يصل إلى 113 ألف طن سنويا، وبقيمة سوقية تناهز 100 مليون دينار، ذلك أنّها تتلف 15.7 بالمائة من إجمالي شراءاتها من الخبز.

English gloss: INC studies show bread waste by Tunisian households (2.7 million households) reaches 113 thousand tonnes a year, worth about 100 million dinars, as households throw away 15.7% of the bread they buy.

> ويقدر حجم التبذير المسجل في المخابز المصنفة، وعددها 3170 مخبزة في نهاية 2017، بـ686 ألف طن من الفارينة المعدة لصنع الخبز، أي 10.4 بالمائة من إجمالي الكميات الموزعة من الفارينة المدعمّة.

English gloss: Waste in classified bakeries (3,170 at end-2017) is put at 686 thousand tonnes of bread flour, 10.4% of subsidised flour distributed.

> ويناهز حجم التبذير الغذائي على مستوى المطاعم الجامعية 11 بالمائة من إجمالي ما يتم إعداده للطلبة، أي حوالي 3 ملايين دينار، سنويا، في حين يعادل التبذير الغذائي في المطاعم الخاصة 16 بالمائة من إجمالي ما يتم إعداده.

English gloss: University canteens waste about 11% of food prepared (about 3 MD a year); private restaurants 16%.

> وأكّد بن جازية، البعد الاقتصادي للتبذير الغذائي، إذ أنّ الخبز يعد من أبرز المنتجات التي يتم تبذيرها، رغم استفادته بدعم سنوي هام من ميزانية الدولة (450 مليون دينار سنة 2017)، كما أنّ تونس تورد حوالي 80 بالمائة من حاجياتها من القمح اللين

English gloss: The INC director stressed that bread is among the most wasted products despite an annual state subsidy of 450 million dinars in 2017, and that Tunisia imports about 80% of its soft wheat needs.
resolvedSources.notes:
- Press relay of INC statements; the underlying INC studies were not available.
- The bakery figure is doubtful as printed: 686 thousand tonnes of flour being 10.4% would imply about 6.6 million tonnes of subsidised flour, while total soft wheat handled is around 1.2 million tonnes a year (11.6 million quintals in 2016, SRC-TG-901 Tableau 11). A unit error (for example 68.6 thousand tonnes) is likely. Not used as an indicator.
- The French-language Kapitalis version of the same dispatch labels 113,000 tonnes as total household food waste rather than bread waste; the Arabic version attributes it to bread.

resolvedSources.title: Gaspillage alimentaire : des pertes annuelles de 570 millions de dinars
resolvedSources.extracts:
Article of 13 December 2018:

> Lors de sa présence à une conférence régionale organisée récemment par la FAO, le ministre du Commerce, Omar El Béhi, a fait savoir que le gaspillage alimentaire provoque annuellement des pertes excédant 570 millions de dinars.

> En 2017, une étude réalisée conjointement par la FAO, le ministère de l'Agriculture et les Ressources Hydrauliques et l'Institut national de la consommation (INC) a estimé le gaspillage alimentaire- au niveau des restaurants universitaires- à une moyenne de 6% des plats jetés.

> Les taux de pertes post-récolte des céréales varient en moyenne de 3,6% dans la région de Bizerte à 5,4% au niveau de Siliana. Pour la chaîne de valeur lait, les taux de perte sont en moyenne de 9% à Bizerte et 6.5% à Mahdia.

> Le projet lancé en 2016 a entamé en 2018 une deuxième phase portant sur le renforcement des capacités des gestionnaires de restaurants universitaires, des boulangers et des enseignants d'écoles et sur la sensibilisation des élèves et des femmes, notamment les femmes rurales.

English gloss: The Minister of Trade said food waste causes losses exceeding 570 MD a year. A 2017 FAO/ministry/INC study put waste in university canteens at 6% of dishes. Post-harvest cereal losses average 3.6% in Bizerte to 5.4% in Siliana; milk chain losses average 9% in Bizerte and 6.5% in Mahdia. The project started in 2016 and began a second phase in 2018.
resolvedSources.notes:
- Press, tier C. The university canteen figure (6%) conflicts with the 11% given by INC via TAP the month before (SRC-TG-907).
- The cereal rates conflict with SRC-TG-908 (4.6% to 7.3% at farm level).

resolvedSources.title: Les chiffres alarmants du gaspillage alimentaire chez les ménages
resolvedSources.extracts:
Article of 7 June 2026:

> Le gaspillage alimentaire coûte chaque année 570 millions de dinars à la Tunisie, poussant le pays à accélérer la mise en place d'une feuille de route d'urgence. Dans cette optique, l'Institut national de la consommation (INC) organise deux ateliers stratégiques les 10 et 17 juin 2026 pour jeter les bases d'une stratégie nationale de lutte contre ce fléau, assortie d'un plan d'action concret et d'un dispositif d'évaluation.

> Cette démarche s'inscrit dans un processus rigoureux supervisé par le ministère du Commerce et du Développement des exportations, en partenariat avec l'Organisation des Nations Unies pour l'alimentation et l'agriculture (FAO). Initié en février 2025, le projet a vu la validation de son rapport de diagnostic le 13 mai 2026

> Les données chiffrées de l'INC illustrent la gravité de la situation, les ménages tunisiens consacrant en moyenne 5 % de leur budget mensuel à de la nourriture jetée. Le pain reste le produit le plus sacrifié : une famille tunisienne gaspille en moyenne 42 kilogrammes de pain par an, ce qui représente 900 000 pièces jetées par jour à l'échelle nationale, soit un gouffre financier de 100 millions de dinars par an. Au quotidien, les ménages gaspillent également 16 % du pain acheté, 10 % des pâtes et céréales, et 6,5 % des légumes.

English gloss: Food waste costs Tunisia 570 MD a year. The INC is holding two workshops (10 and 17 June 2026) to lay the basis of a national strategy against food waste, under the Ministry of Trade with FAO; the project started in February 2025 and its diagnostic report was validated on 13 May 2026. INC data: households spend 5% of their monthly budget on food thrown away; 42 kg of bread per family per year, 900,000 loaves a day nationally, 100 MD a year; 16% of bread bought, 10% of pasta and cereals and 6.5% of vegetables are wasted.
resolvedSources.notes:
- The figures repeat the 2014-2016 INC estimates (SRC-TG-906) without a new survey date; they are not evidence of the 2026 level.
- The article also quotes Ramadan figures (66.6% cooked dishes, 46% bread) as "taux de gaspillage"; the 2017 report (SRC-TG-906) shows these are shares of respondents naming the item, not waste rates.
- The diagnostic report validated in May 2026 was not found online.

resolvedSources.title: Understanding Bread Consumption and Waste Patterns in Algeria and Tunisia: Insights into Consumer Practices and Challenges
resolvedSources.publisher: North African Journal of Food and Nutrition Research 9(20):193-218 (Bouledroua D., Debbabi H., Khaled M.B., Ben Ismail H., Jribi S., Doggui D., Sfayhi Terras D.)
resolvedSources.extracts:
PDF downloaded from https://najfnr.com/home/article/download/730/405/5598 (page numbers below are PDF pages of that file).

Abstract, PDF p. 1:

> A cross-sectional study was conducted employing an online survey administered between September and December 2023. The study population comprised 636 respondents: 316 Algerian participants (62.8% female, 64.9% aged 25–60 years, 76% with university education) and 320 Tunisian participants (76.3% female, 76.2% aged 25–60 years, 90% with university education).

> Interestingly, bread wastage, while limited, was attributed to sensory deficiencies, including staleness, suboptimal taste, and poor texture. Inaccurate quantity estimation and subsidized bread prices were identified as leading causes of waste in both countries. Despite the majority of respondents reporting the storage of leftover bread, occasional discarding remained prevalent, with 6.5% of Algerian respondents and 5.8% of Tunisian respondents consistently discarding stored bread.

Introduction, PDF p. 3:

> Similarly, in Tunisia, the INC (2025) estimates annual bread waste at around 113,000 tonnes, representing approximately 16% of household bread expenditure and 5% of total household food expenditure.

Methods, PDF p. 3: "Data collection occurred between September and December 2023, using a convenience sample."

Results, PDF p. 20:

> The most frequently cited reason was the incorrect estimation of the quantity purchased relative to daily needs, reported by 51.5% of Algerian and 61.5% of Tunisian respondents. This was followed by governmental subsidies of bread, identified by 16.8% of Algerian and 14.1 % of Tunisian respondents, and concerns over bread quality, mentioned by 14.2% of Algerian and 12.8% of Tunisian respondents. Poor storage practices were cited by 9.9% of Algerian and 9% of Tunisian respondents. Over-production accounted for 7.6% of responses of the Algerian, while it was reported by only 2.6% of Tunisian respondents.

Discussion, PDF p. 21:

> Governmental subsidies, while intended to ensure affordability, might also inadvertently encourage overbuying and less responsible consumption (Khader et al., 2019; Obeidat et al., 2015), although the study found no direct correlation between perceived price and waste, suggesting that the issue is more complex than just cost

English gloss: Online convenience survey of 320 Tunisians (Sept-Dec 2023, mostly women and university-educated). Bread waste is "limited"; 5.8% of Tunisian respondents consistently discard stored bread. Causes named by Tunisian respondents: misjudging quantity 61.5%, government subsidies 14.1%, bread quality 12.8%, poor storage 9%, over-production 2.6%. The authors found no direct correlation between perceived price and waste. They cite INC (2025) for 113,000 t a year of bread waste, about 16% of household bread expenditure and 5% of food expenditure.
resolvedSources.notes:
- The 113,000 t / 16% / 5% figures are cited from INC, not measured by the authors; one co-author is affiliated with the INC. They are a peer-reviewed restatement of the INC figures, not independent confirmation.
- Note the base: here 16% is of bread expenditure, while other sources say 15.7-16% of bread purchased.
- The convenience sample is skewed (90% university-educated, 76% women), so its own shares are not nationally representative.
- DOI inconsistency in the PDF: the header prints 10.51745/najfnr.9.20.193-218, the citation box gives 10.51745/najfnr.9.19.193-218 (used here as url).

relatedItems.title: The state cereal system (Office des Céréales monopoly, decreed prices, CGC subsidies) built in 1962-1971 now strains public finances and blunts market signals
Tunisia imports roughly half of its cereals and almost all of its soft (bread) wheat, even in good harvest years

Cereal losses at harvest, on-farm storage and collection are linked to poorly set harvesting machinery, an old farm machinery stock and open-air storage, but have been measured only once, in two governorates
